title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (1 of 7)
hook: a boy watches his father give away worn-out cows, and asks one question too many
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Last week, tadvana, the dear one: the gods' victory was never theirs. It was Brahman's, the one behind the ear.

A charity drive at a big house. The owner is making a show of generosity, and his servants lead the gifts out one by one. But the kid in the doorway notices something. The gifts are the old stuff: cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and will never calf again. Everyone else nods politely. The boy can't. So begins the Katha Upanishad: a boy named Nachiketa, a father's careless gift, and, before long, Death.
screen: `A SHOW OF GENEROSITY.` → `THE OLD COWS.` → `THE BOY IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The father, Vajashravasa, is performing a sacrifice where you're meant to give away everything you own. But his cows are worn out. The text says it bluntly: they've drunk their water, eaten their grass, been milked dry, and will bear no more. Joyless worlds, it says, await the one who gives gifts like these. Then: shraddha entered the boy. Shraddha is faith, trust, a deep seriousness; you met it in the Gita. It enters Nachiketa, still a child, and he goes to his father. Father, to whom will you give me? If the sacrifice means giving everything, the son belongs on the list. It's a real question, and a sharp one. The father doesn't answer. Nachiketa asks a second time, then a third. And the father, angry, the way a parent can be when a child sees through them in front of others, snaps: I give you to Death. To Yama. It's an ancient story, and a very modern one. A parent says something in anger they can't take back, and a child takes them at their word. Nachiketa doesn't run and hide. He thinks it through: I go first among many, in the middle of many. What will Yama do with me? He sees that people ripen and fall like grain, and rise again like grain. And he goes. This week is the Katha, and its big idea is the two paths; they arrive in two days. It starts with a boy who couldn't pretend old cows were a gift.
screen: `THE WORN-OUT COWS.` · `SHRADDHA ENTERED THE BOY.` · `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` · `I GIVE YOU TO DEATH.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've given lately, time, money, attention, help, and ask gently, without blame: was it a real gift, or a worn-out one, the leftover hour, the distracted ear, the thing you didn't want anyway? Then hold one real thing you could give this week, something that would cost you a little, and breathe with it.
Nachiketa. A boy whose father, angry, said: I give you to Death. Shraddha, faith, had entered him, and he went to Yama's house without fear.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. The boy saw what everyone else nodded past. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus tell the Katha's story of Nachiketa to children and also study it closely; Vedanta teachers, Shankara among them, wrote commentaries on it.

fork.setup: you're a child watching your father give away worthless cows as if they were a great gift. what do you do?
options: say nothing; it's not your place.
ask him: to whom will you give me?
fork.reveal: Nachiketa asks, three times. his father snaps: to Death I give you. and the boy goes.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nachiketa (stem nachiketas), the boy at the heart of the Katha.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a story about a cruel father.
what it means: it starts with a false gift and a child whose shraddha won't let it pass.
what a scholar hears: the Katha expands a shorter Nachiketas story in the Taittiriya Brahmana (3.11.8), where the father's words are also 'to Death I give you'.
